mainEntity.name: How often does a tennis court need cleaning?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Annually for most, and the sensible time is before the season rather than after it. A court under heavy tree cover, which is most suburban Melbourne courts, is closer to twice a year on the shaded end alone.

Synthetic surfaces benefit from a mid year pass purely for the infill, separate from the growth question.

mainEntity.name: Will cleaning damage the line marking?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Not at the pressure these surfaces are cleaned at. Line marking is the reason the pressure is kept low, along with the acrylic texture itself.

Marking that is already failing will look worse once the surrounding surface is clean, which is not damage but is worth expecting. It is usually a sign the court is approaching a resurface.

mainEntity.name: Can you clean a synthetic grass court?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Yes, and it is a different job to a hard court. The work is lifting and redistributing the infill and treating growth in the pile, rather than washing a surface.

What we will not do is pressure clean it, because that blows infill out of the pile and the court then needs topping up, which costs more than the clean did.

mainEntity.name: How long is the court out of use?

acceptedAnswer.text:
Usually the day it is done plus drying time. A hard court is playable once it is dry, which on a mild day is a few hours and after rain is longer.

Where a treatment is applied for moss or lichen, there is a dwell period before rinsing and the court stays closed through it.

No. Moss and algae come back wherever the conditions that grew them are still there, which on a shaded court with trees overhead they will be.

What changes the interval is dealing with the cause: clearing the drainage, cutting back what is overhanging, and treating rather than just washing. Mould, algae, moss and lichen treatment explains how the treatment works.
